claim: CelTOS is conserved in apicomplexan parasites of the genera Plasmodium, Babesia, Cytauxzoon and Theileria.
source: We found CelTOS is conserved across various diverse branches of apicomplexan parasites including the hemosporidia (Plasmodium spp.) and piroplasms (Theileria, Babesia, Cytauxzoon spp.), groups that are thought to have diverged more than 100 million years ago (DeBarry and Kissinger, 2011) (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and cited reference to evolutionary divergence.

claim: Apicomplexan parasites with CelTOS diverged more than 100 million years ago.
source: We found CelTOS is conserved across various diverse branches of apicomplexan parasites including the hemosporidia (Plasmodium spp.) and piroplasms (Theileria, Babesia, Cytauxzoon spp.), groups that are thought to have diverged more than 100 million years ago (DeBarry and Kissinger, 2011) (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to DeBarry and Kissinger, 2011.

claim: CelTOS is absent in Toxoplasma gondii.
source: This is supported by the lack of CelTOS in the apicomplexan Toxoplasma gondii that does not require an arthropod vector for transmission.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript text.

claim: Toxoplasma gondii does not require an arthropod vector for transmission.
source: This is supported by the lack of CelTOS in the apicomplexan Toxoplasma gondii that does not require an arthropod vector for transmission.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about T. gondii biology.

claim: PvCelTOS forms an alpha helical dimer that resembles a tuning fork.
source: CelTOS forms an alpha helical dimer that resembles a tuning fork (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The CelTOS dimer has a buried surface area of 3003 Å2.
source: The dimer has a large buried surface area of 3003 Å2.
evidence: Calculated from structural data.

claim: CelTOS is an obligate dimer in solution.
source: Consistent with the structure and large buried surface area, we established that CelTOS is an obligate dimer in solution by sedimentation equilibrium analytical ultracentrifugation (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation experiments.

claim: The outer surface of the CelTOS dimer is mildly hydrophilic.
source: The outer surface of the CelTOS dimer is mildly hydrophilic (Figure 1C and E)
evidence: Supported by electrostatic surface potential maps shown in Figure 1C and E.

claim: CelTOS has inner hydrophobic surfaces created between the two tines of the dimer and the dimer interface.
source: The outer surface of the CelTOS dimer is mildly hydrophilic (Figure 1C and E) and masks inner hydrophobic surfaces created between the two tines of the CelTOS dimer and the dimer interface (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by surface maps shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The C-terminal helices of CelTOS show structural similarity to HIV-1 gp41.
source: The C-terminal helices of CelTOS show structural similarity to HIV-1 gp41 (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by structural overlay shown in Figure 2A and DALI server comparison.

claim: The C-terminal helices of CelTOS show structural similarity to Mycobacterium bovis ESAT-6.
source: The C-terminal helices of CelTOS show structural similarity to HIV-1 gp41 (Figure 2A) and Mycobacterium bovis ESAT-6 (Figure 2D)
evidence: Supported by structural overlay shown in Figure 2D and DALI server comparison.

claim: The N-terminal helices of CelTOS show structural similarity to Hendravirus fusion core.
source: the N-terminal helices show similarity to Hendravirus fusion core (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by structural overlay shown in Figure 2B and DALI server comparison.

claim: The N-terminal helices of CelTOS show structural similarity to Nipahvirus fusion subunit core.
source: the N-terminal helices show similarity to Hendravirus fusion core (Figure 2B); Nipahvirus fusion subunit core (Figure 2C) (Buzon et al., 2010; Lou et al., 2006; Renshaw et al., 2005; Hsu et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by structural overlay shown in Figure 2C and cited references.

claim: PfCelTOS demonstrates significant binding to phosphatidic acid (PA).
source: Both P. falciparum (Pf) and P. vivax (Pv) CelTOS demonstrated significant binding to phosphatidic acid (PA) (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by spotted lipid array data shown in Figure 3.

claim: PvCelTOS demonstrates significant binding to phosphatidic acid (PA).
source: Both P. falciparum (Pf) and P. vivax (Pv) CelTOS demonstrated significant binding to phosphatidic acid (PA) (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by spotted lipid array data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Phosphatidic acid is predominantly found on the inner leaflet of plasma membranes.
source: Phosphatidic acid is predominantly found on the inner leaflet of plasma membranes (Op den Kamp, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Op den Kamp, 1979.

claim: PvCelTOS binds to cardiolipin.
source: Specific binding of PvCelTOS to cardiolipin was also observed.
evidence: Observed in lipid binding assays.

claim: Cardiolipin binding is not conserved between PfCelTOS and PvCelTOS.
source: However, the relevance of this binding specificity is unclear as it is not conserved in CelTOS from both P. falciparum and P. vivax.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of binding data between PfCelTOS and PvCelTOS.

claim: CelTOS shows limited or undetectable binding to sphingomyelin (SM).
source: Limited or undetectable binding was observed to phospholipids predominantly found on the outer leaflet of plasma membranes including sphingomyelin (SM) and phosphatidylcholine (PC) (Op den Kamp, 1979).
evidence: Supported by lipid binding assay data.

claim: CelTOS shows limited or undetectable binding to phosphatidylcholine (PC).
source: Limited or undetectable binding was observed to phospholipids predominantly found on the outer leaflet of plasma membranes including sphingomyelin (SM) and phosphatidylcholine (PC) (Op den Kamp, 1979).
evidence: Supported by lipid binding assay data.

claim: Sphingomyelin is predominantly found on the outer leaflet of plasma membranes.
source: Limited or undetectable binding was observed to phospholipids predominantly found on the outer leaflet of plasma membranes including sphingomyelin (SM) and phosphatidylcholine (PC) (Op den Kamp, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Op den Kamp, 1979.

claim: Phosphatidylcholine is predominantly found on the outer leaflet of plasma membranes.
source: Limited or undetectable binding was observed to phospholipids predominantly found on the outer leaflet of plasma membranes including sphingomyelin (SM) and phosphatidylcholine (PC) (Op den Kamp, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Op den Kamp, 1979.

claim: CelTOS has enhanced specificity for the cytosolic face of cell membranes.
source: These results demonstrate that CelTOS has enhanced specificity for the cytosolic face of cell membranes
evidence: Inferred from preferential binding to inner leaflet lipids (PA) over outer leaflet lipids (PC, SM).

claim: CelTOS possesses a specific binding pocket that preferentially accommodates PA over the headgroups of other phospholipids.
source: These results demonstrate that CelTOS has enhanced specificity for the cytosolic face of cell membranes and suggests CelTOS possesses a specific binding pocket that preferentially accommodates PA over the headgroups of other phospholipids.
evidence: Inferred from the specific binding pattern to PA versus other phospholipids.

claim: Nanomolar concentrations of CelTOS disrupt PA liposomes.
source: Nanomolar concentrations of CelTOS disrupted PA liposomes consistent with a potent role in the disruption of PA containing membranes (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by liposome disruption assay data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Minimal disruption of PS liposomes by CelTOS was observed and required micromolar concentrations.
source: In contrast, minimal disruption of PS and PC liposomes by CelTOS was observed and this required micromolar concentrations of CelTOS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by liposome disruption assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Minimal disruption of PC liposomes by CelTOS was observed and required micromolar concentrations.
source: In contrast, minimal disruption of PS and PC liposomes by CelTOS was observed and this required micromolar concentrations of CelTOS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by liposome disruption assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: E. coli IspF does not disrupt liposomes.
source: Liposome disruption was specific to CelTOS as addition of the control protein E. coli IspF, that has similar mass, isoelectric point and purification method as CelTOS, had no effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by negative control data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The CelTOS protein alone is necessary and sufficient for membrane disruption.
source: These results demonstrate that the CelTOS protein alone is necessary and sufficient for membrane disruption
evidence: Inferred from liposome disruption assays showing CelTOS activity and lack of activity with control protein.

claim: CelTOS specifically targets inner leaflet phosphatidic acid lipid compositions.
source: These results demonstrate that the CelTOS protein alone is necessary and sufficient for membrane disruption, specifically targets inner leaflet phosphatidic acid lipid compositions
evidence: Inferred from preferential disruption of PA liposomes over PS and PC liposomes.

claim: CelTOS has a conserved membrane disruption function across Plasmodium species.
source: These results demonstrate that the CelTOS protein alone is necessary and sufficient for membrane disruption, specifically targets inner leaflet phosphatidic acid lipid compositions, and has a conserved function across Plasmodium spp.
evidence: Inferred from similar liposome disruption activity of both PfCelTOS and PvCelTOS.

claim: Only 500 kDa dextran blocks carboxyfluorescein release from liposomes disrupted by PfCelTOS.
source: Remarkably, only the 500 kDa dextran blocked carboxyfluorescein release from liposomes disrupted with PfCelTOS and PvCelTOS, respectively (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by dextran blocking experiments shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Only 500 kDa dextran blocks carboxyfluorescein release from liposomes disrupted by PvCelTOS.
source: Remarkably, only the 500 kDa dextran blocked carboxyfluorescein release from liposomes disrupted with PfCelTOS and PvCelTOS, respectively (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by dextran blocking experiments shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Dextran molecules of higher and lower molecular weights than 500 kDa had no effect on carboxyfluorescein release.
source: Dextran molecules of higher and lower molecular weights and Stoke's radius had no effect on carboxyfluorescein release, similar to experiments without dextran.
evidence: Supported by dextran blocking experiments.

claim: 500 kDa dextran has the correct Stoke's radius to occupy the CelTOS pore.
source: Therefore, only the 500 kDa dextran has the correct Stoke's radius to occupy the pore, while the remaining dextran molecules are either too small and diffuse through the pore or too large and may not enter the pore.
evidence: Inferred from the selective blocking effect of 500 kDa dextran.

claim: 500 kDa dextran significantly lowered the maximum amount of carboxyfluorescein released compared to experiments with molecules of higher and lower molecular weights or without dextran.
source: The 500 kDa dextran significantly lowered the maximum amount of carboxyfluorescein released disrupted (A, in Equation 2) compared to experiments with molecules of higher and lower molecular weights, or without dextran (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: CelTOS forms pores of uniform size in liposomes.
source: This suggests that CelTOS forms pores of uniform size in liposomes
evidence: Inferred from the specific blocking by a single dextran size.

claim: The average diameter of pores formed by PfCelTOS is 45.85 ± 15.55 nm.
source: The average diameter of the pores, reported as mean ± s.d., formed by PfCelTOS and PvCelTOS were 45.85 ± 15.55 nm and 58.62 ± 21.86 nm respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Measured by transmission electron microscopy as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The average diameter of pores formed by PvCelTOS is 58.62 ± 21.86 nm.
source: The average diameter of the pores, reported as mean ± s.d., formed by PfCelTOS and PvCelTOS were 45.85 ± 15.55 nm and 58.62 ± 21.86 nm respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Measured by transmission electron microscopy as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: CelTOS forms pores visible by transmission electron microscopy.
source: We visualized the CelTOS-pore in liposomes by transmission electron microscopy of negative stained liposomes (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Microinjection of PfCelTOS into Xenopus oocytes causes membrane damage.
source: In contrast, microinjection of Pf or PvCelTOS caused significant increase in the number of cells that had damaged membranes (Figure 6A and B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by microinjection experiments shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Microinjection of PvCelTOS into Xenopus oocytes causes membrane damage.
source: In contrast, microinjection of Pf or PvCelTOS caused significant increase in the number of cells that had damaged membranes (Figure 6A and B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by microinjection experiments shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Microinjection of buffer into Xenopus oocytes causes only minor membrane phenotypes.
source: Only minor membrane phenotypes due to the injection process were observed in oocytes injected with buffer and in those injected with the negative control protein, EcIspF.
evidence: Supported by negative control data from microinjection experiments.

claim: Microinjection of EcIspF into Xenopus oocytes causes only minor membrane phenotypes.
source: Only minor membrane phenotypes due to the injection process were observed in oocytes injected with buffer and in those injected with the negative control protein, EcIspF.
evidence: Supported by negative control data from microinjection experiments.

claim: CelTOS is unable to disrupt RAW 264.7 macrophages from the extracellular surface.
source: No membrane disruption, measured by uptake of a membrane-impermeable fluorescent dye, was observed for macrophages in tissue culture when CelTOS was added to the extracellular media (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: CelTOS is incapable of disrupting plasma membranes from the extracellular face because it does not bind phospholipids found predominantly in the outer leaflet of plasma membranes.
source: This is fully consistent as CelTOS does not bind phospholipids found predominantly in the outer leaflet of plasma membranes, rendering it incapable of disrupting plasma membranes from the extracellular face (Figure 3, Figure 6C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Inferred from lipid binding specificity and lack of extracellular membrane disruption activity.

claim: CelTOS is the only parasite protein known to breach plasma membranes from the cytoplasmic face to enable the exit of parasites from cells during traversal.
source: We have identified CelTOS as the only parasite protein known to breach plasma membranes from the cytoplasmic face to enable the exit of parasites from cells during traversal.
evidence: Inferred from the unique inner leaflet targeting and membrane disruption activity of CelTOS.

claim: CelTOS is released from parasite secretory organelles and adheres to the surface of the malaria parasite prior to and during the traversal of host and vector cells.
source: CelTOS is released from parasite secretory organelles and adheres to the surface of the malaria parasite prior to and during the traversal of host and vector cells (Bergmann-Leitner et al., 2010, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bergmann-Leitner et al., 2010, 2011.

claim: When the parasite is extracellular, CelTOS has limited cell membrane disrupting activity due to its low preference for lipids on the outer surface of plasma membranes.
source: Our results show that when the parasite is extracellular, CelTOS has limited cell membrane disrupting activity due to its low preference for lipids on the outer surface of plasma membranes.
evidence: Inferred from lipid binding specificity and liposome disruption data.

claim: Once the parasite invades the cytosol of host and vector cells, CelTOS binds with high specificity to lipids in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: Once the parasite invades the cytosol of host and vector cells, CelTOS binds with high specificity to lipids in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
evidence: Inferred from PA binding specificity and inner leaflet localization of PA.

claim: CelTOS binding to inner leaflet lipids leads to localized membrane disruption and pore formation.
source: Binding leads to localized membrane disruption and pore formation that creates a portal to ultimately direct the exit of the parasite from the host or vector cells to complete traversal.
evidence: Inferred from liposome disruption and pore formation data.

claim: CelTOS is essential for traversal of malaria parasites in both the mosquito vector and human host.
source: Cell-traversal protein for ookinetes and sporozoites (CelTOS) is unique among traversal proteins as it is essential for traversal of malaria parasites in both the mosquito vector and human host and is therefore critical for malaria transmission and disease pathogenesis (Kariu et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kariu et al., 2006.

claim: CelTOS is critical for malaria transmission and disease pathogenesis.
source: Cell-traversal protein for ookinetes and sporozoites (CelTOS) is unique among traversal proteins as it is essential for traversal of malaria parasites in both the mosquito vector and human host and is therefore critical for malaria transmission and disease pathogenesis (Kariu et al., 2006).
evidence: Inferred from its essential role in traversal in both vector and host.

claim: CelTOS has been identified as a promising malaria vaccine candidate referred to as Antigen 2.
source: Additionally, CelTOS has been identified as a promising malaria vaccine candidate referred to as Antigen 2 (Doolan et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doolan et al., 2003.

claim: Immunization of mice with recombinant CelTOS results in humoral and cellular immune responses that reduced infection.
source: Immunization of mice with recombinant CelTOS results in humoral and cellular immune responses that reduced infection, demonstrating that targeting CelTOS is a viable approach for developing a malaria vaccine (Bergmann-Leitner et al., 2010; Ferraro et al., 2013; Bergmann-Leitner et al., 2011, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bergmann-Leitner et al., 2010; Ferraro et al., 2013; Bergmann-Leitner et al., 2011, 2013.

claim: Targeting CelTOS is a viable approach for developing a malaria vaccine.
source: Immunization of mice with recombinant CelTOS results in humoral and cellular immune responses that reduced infection, demonstrating that targeting CelTOS is a viable approach for developing a malaria vaccine (Bergmann-Leitner et al., 2010; Ferraro et al., 2013; Bergmann-Leitner et al., 2011, 2013).
evidence: Inferred from successful immunization studies cited.

claim: CelTOS has no sequence similarity to proteins of known function.
source: Even though CelTOS is critical during cell traversal by malaria parasites and is a leading transmission- and infection-blocking malaria vaccine candidate, its function remains unknown as it has no sequence similarity to proteins of known function.
evidence: Stated as a fact based on sequence analysis.

claim: CelTOS structurally resembles viral membrane fusion proteins and a bacterial pore-forming toxin.
source: CelTOS structurally resembles viral membrane fusion proteins and a bacterial pore-forming toxin.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison using DALI server.

claim: CelTOS specifically binds phosphatidic acid.
source: We show that CelTOS specifically binds phosphatidic acid, a lipid predominantly found in the inner leaflet of plasma membranes
evidence: Supported by lipid binding assays.

claim: CelTOS potently disrupts defined liposomes composed of phosphatidic acid.
source: We show that CelTOS specifically binds phosphatidic acid, a lipid predominantly found in the inner leaflet of plasma membranes, and potently disrupts defined liposomes composed of phosphatidic acid.
evidence: Supported by liposome disruption assays.

claim: Liposome disruption by CelTOS is achieved by the formation of CelTOS-dependent pores.
source: We determine that liposome disruption is achieved by the formation of CelTOS-dependent pores.
evidence: Supported by dextran blocking experiments and electron microscopy.

claim: Microinjection of CelTOS into Xenopus oocytes results in membrane damage.
source: Additionally, microinjection of CelTOS into Xenopus oocytes results in membrane damage.
evidence: Supported by microinjection experiments.

claim: CelTOS is the only known apicomplexan protein with universal inner leaflet cellular activity.
source: Together, these results demonstrate CelTOS is the only known apicomplexan protein with universal inner leaflet cellular activity as it addresses phosphatidic acid found specifically on the cytoplasmic face of plasma membranes, and disrupts these membranes to enable the exit of apicomplexan parasites through diverse vector and host cells.
evidence: Inferred from the unique combination of inner leaflet targeting and membrane disruption activity.

claim: CelTOS addresses phosphatidic acid found specifically on the cytoplasmic face of plasma membranes.
source: Together, these results demonstrate CelTOS is the only known apicomplexan protein with universal inner leaflet cellular activity as it addresses phosphatidic acid found specifically on the cytoplasmic face of plasma membranes
evidence: Supported by PA binding specificity and inner leaflet localization.

claim: CelTOS disrupts membranes to enable the exit of apicomplexan parasites through diverse vector and host cells.
source: Together, these results demonstrate CelTOS is the only known apicomplexan protein with universal inner leaflet cellular activity as it addresses phosphatidic acid found specifically on the cytoplasmic face of plasma membranes, and disrupts these membranes to enable the exit of apicomplexan parasites through diverse vector and host cells.
evidence: Inferred from membrane disruption activity and known role in cell traversal.

claim: The structure of CelTOS is unique and distinct from viral and bacterial membrane disruption proteins.
source: While CelTOS resembles these viral and bacterial proteins, the CelTOS structure is unique and distinct as it contains two independent subdomains that both could act as membrane disruption modules.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis showing two subdomains with similarity to different membrane disruption proteins.

claim: CelTOS contains two independent subdomains that both could act as membrane disruption modules.
source: While CelTOS resembles these viral and bacterial proteins, the CelTOS structure is unique and distinct as it contains two independent subdomains that both could act as membrane disruption modules.
evidence: Inferred from structural similarity of N-terminal and C-terminal helices to different membrane disruption proteins.

claim: The N-terminal and C-terminal helices in CelTOS resemble heptad repeats that form helices in class I viral fusion proteins.
source: Both the N-terminal and C-terminal helices in CelTOS resemble the heptad repeats that form helices in class I viral fusion proteins (Figure 2A–C) (Sackett and Shai, 2002; Harrison, 2015; LeDuc and Shin, 2000).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison and citations.

claim: Viral heptad repeats undergo conformational changes that enhance the destabilization of host membranes post-insertion of the viral fusion peptide.
source: Viral heptad repeats undergo conformational changes that enhance the destabilization of host membranes post-insertion of the viral fusion peptide that enables lipid mixing during fusion(38).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about viral fusion proteins.

claim: The N- and C-terminal helices in CelTOS may undergo conformational changes during membrane disruption.
source: It is plausible that the N- and C-terminal helices in CelTOS may also undergo similar conformational changes during membrane disruption.
evidence: Speculated based on similarity to viral fusion proteins.

claim: CelTOS employs a distinct membrane disruption mechanism from viral proteins as lipid mixing is not required.
source: However, CelTOS employs a distinct membrane disruption mechanism from viral proteins as lipid mixing is not required for CelTOS to target inner leaflet lipids and disrupt plasma membranes.
evidence: Inferred from the mechanism of CelTOS action targeting inner leaflet from cytoplasm.

claim: CelTOS is structurally similar to the pore-forming toxin M. tuberculosis ESAT-6.
source: In addition, CelTOS is structurally similar to the pore-forming toxin M. tuberculosis ESAT-6 (Figure 2D) (Hsu et al., 2003; Los et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison and citations.

claim: Pore-forming toxins generally recognize a host cell target or receptor embedded within the target membrane.
source: However, these toxins generally recognize a host cell target or receptor embedded within the target membrane
evidence: Stated as general knowledge about pore-forming toxins.

claim: ESAT-6 is secreted in complex with a chaperone that maintains it in an inactive state.
source: However, these toxins generally recognize a host cell target or receptor embedded within the target membrane, and ESAT-6 is secreted in complex with a chaperone that maintains it in an inactive state.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about ESAT-6.

claim: Upon binding the membrane target, ESAT-6 sheds the chaperone, oligomerizes and embeds into the membrane to form a pore.
source: Upon binding the membrane target, the toxin sheds the chaperone, oligomerizes and embeds into the membrane to form a pore on the angstrom length scale for the passage of ions and water (Los et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Los et al., 2013.

claim: The dimeric nature of CelTOS may serve as a chaperone-like function to retain CelTOS in an inactive state prior to membrane binding.
source: The dimeric nature of CelTOS may serve as a chaperone-like function to retain CelTOS in an inactive state prior to membrane binding as the dimer masks the inner hydrophobic faces of CelTOS.
evidence: Speculated based on structural features and comparison to ESAT-6.

claim: The CelTOS dimer masks the inner hydrophobic faces of CelTOS.
source: The dimeric nature of CelTOS may serve as a chaperone-like function to retain CelTOS in an inactive state prior to membrane binding as the dimer masks the inner hydrophobic faces of CelTOS.
evidence: Inferred from structural data showing hydrophobic surfaces at dimer interface.

claim: Malaria continues to be a global health problem, with half of the world's population at risk.
source: Malaria continues to be a global health problem, with half of the world's population at risk.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about malaria epidemiology.

claim: The lack of an effective vaccine against malaria and the continuous evolution of drug-resistant parasites make malaria control difficult.
source: The lack of an effective vaccine against malaria, and the continuous evolution of drug-resistant parasites make malaria control difficult.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about malaria control challenges.

claim: Targeting the liver-stage is of high priority for malaria vaccine development.
source: Targeting the liver-stage (Good and Doolan, 1999) and mosquito-stages (mCGo, 2011) are of high priority for malaria vaccine development.
evidence: Supported by citations to Good and Doolan, 1999.

claim: Targeting the mosquito-stage is of high priority for malaria vaccine development.
source: Targeting the liver-stage (Good and Doolan, 1999) and mosquito-stages (mCGo, 2011) are of high priority for malaria vaccine development.
evidence: Supported by citations to mCGo, 2011.

claim: Immunization of human volunteers with radiation-attenuated sporozoites induces sterile immunity.
source: Immunization of human volunteers with radiation-attenuated sporozoites induces sterile immunity (Good and Doolan, 1999; Hoffman et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to Good and Doolan, 1999; Hoffman et al., 2002.

claim: All volunteers immunized with radiation-attenuated sporozoites showed strong immune responses to CelTOS that were correlated with protection.
source: and all volunteers showed strong immune responses to CelTOS (referred to as Antigen 2) that were correlated with protection (Doolan et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doolan et al., 2003.

claim: Circumsporozoite protein was only recognized by a third of volunteers immunized with radiation-attenuated sporozoites and mostly in those who were not protected.
source: In contrast, circumsporozoite protein, which is the major component of the most advanced malaria vaccine RTS,S (Crompton et al., 2010), was only recognized by a third of the volunteers and mostly in those who were not protected (Doolan et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doolan et al., 2003.

claim: Circumsporozoite protein is the major component of the most advanced malaria vaccine RTS,S.
source: In contrast, circumsporozoite protein, which is the major component of the most advanced malaria vaccine RTS,S (Crompton et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Crompton et al., 2010.

claim: Individuals living in malaria endemic regions mount IFN-γ responses to CelTOS.
source: Individuals living in malaria endemic regions mount IFN-γ responses to CelTOS suggesting that CelTOS is a target of protective immunity (Anum et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anum et al., 2015.

claim: CelTOS is a target of protective immunity.
source: Individuals living in malaria endemic regions mount IFN-γ responses to CelTOS suggesting that CelTOS is a target of protective immunity (Anum et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from IFN-γ responses in endemic populations.

claim: CelTOS is a promising multi-stage malaria vaccine target for both infection-blocking and transmission-blocking vaccines.
source: CelTOS is also unique as it is a promising multi-stage malaria vaccine target (Bergmann-Leitner et al., 2010; Ferraro et al., 2013; Bergmann-Leitner et al., 2011, 2013) for both infection-blocking and transmission-blocking vaccines currently in clinical trials.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bergmann-Leitner et al., 2010; Ferraro et al., 2013; Bergmann-Leitner et al., 2011, 2013.

claim: CelTOS has conserved critical function in both Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax.
source: We show that CelTOS has conserved critical function in both Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax that infect humans.
evidence: Supported by functional data from both PfCelTOS and PvCelTOS.

claim: The high-sequence similarity between PfCelTOS and PvCelTOS suggests that CelTOS may elicit cross-species protection.
source: The high-sequence similarity between Pf and PvCelTOS suggest that CelTOS may elicit cross-species protection.
evidence: Inferred from sequence similarity and conserved function.

claim: CelTOS could be used alone or in combination with other antigens to produce an effective multicomponent vaccine which targets both the mosquito and human stages and may be cross-species protective.
source: Therefore, CelTOS could be used alone or in combination with other antigens already in development to produce an effective multicomponent vaccine which targets both the mosquito and human stages and may be cross-species protective (Doolan et al., 2003; Crompton et al., 2010; Crosnier et al., 2011).
evidence: Speculated based on CelTOS properties and supported by citations.

claim: CelTOS-based vaccines have demonstrated the ability to elicit protection from malaria infection.
source: CelTOS-based vaccines have demonstrated the ability to elicit protection from malaria infection.
evidence: Stated as established from previous studies.

claim: Protection from CelTOS-based vaccines is not absolute.
source: However, protection is not absolute suggesting improvements in the immunogenicity, protectivity and formulation of CelTOS-based vaccines are necessary.
evidence: Stated as established from previous vaccine studies.

claim: Improvements in the immunogenicity, protectivity and formulation of CelTOS-based vaccines are necessary.
source: However, protection is not absolute suggesting improvements in the immunogenicity, protectivity and formulation of CelTOS-based vaccines are necessary.
evidence: Inferred from incomplete protection observed in vaccine studies.

claim: The structure and architecture of CelTOS provides necessary insight to inform immune recognition.
source: The structure and architecture of CelTOS provides necessary insight to inform immune recognition, and enables protein engineering to retain the structural fold during immunogen design.
evidence: Inferred from the structural data obtained.

claim: The structure of CelTOS enables protein engineering to retain the structural fold during immunogen design.
source: The structure and architecture of CelTOS provides necessary insight to inform immune recognition, and enables protein engineering to retain the structural fold during immunogen design.
evidence: Inferred from structural knowledge enabling rational design.

claim: Perforin-like proteins (PLPs) mediate entry into various pre-erythrocytic cells.
source: The current literature supports a model where perforin-like proteins (PLPs) mediate entry into various pre-erythrocytic cells including the PLP-1 dependent disruption of transient vacuoles created during entry of hepatocytes (Risco-Castillo et al., 2015; Ishino et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Risco-Castillo et al., 2015; Ishino et al., 2005.

claim: PLP-1 dependent disruption of transient vacuoles occurs during entry of hepatocytes.
source: The current literature supports a model where perforin-like proteins (PLPs) mediate entry into various pre-erythrocytic cells including the PLP-1 dependent disruption of transient vacuoles created during entry of hepatocytes (Risco-Castillo et al., 2015; Ishino et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Risco-Castillo et al., 2015; Ishino et al., 2005.

claim: PLPs have been shown to play a role in egress of parasites from the parasitophorous vacuole and red blood cells.
source: Further, PLPs have been shown to play a role in egress of parasites from the parasitophorous vacuole and red blood cells (Garg et al., 2013; Wirth et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garg et al., 2013; Wirth et al., 2014.

claim: Proteins involved in breaching the plasma membrane of invaded cells during traversal from the cytoplasmic face to enable the exit of parasites are unknown.
source: However, proteins involved in breaching the plasma membrane of invaded cells during traversal, from the cytoplasmic face, to enable the exit of parasites are unknown.
evidence: Stated as a gap in knowledge prior to this study.

claim: CelTOS attacks plasma membranes from the cytoplasmic face.
source: We have discovered that secreted apicomplexan CelTOS attacks plasma membranes from the cytoplasmic face.
evidence: Supported by lipid binding specificity and cellular assays.

claim: CelTOS-deficient parasites are unable to traverse cells of their host and vector.
source: CelTOS had previously been identified as a malaria antigen, and CelTOS-deficient parasites are unable to traverse cells of their host and vector (Kariu et al., 2006; Doolan et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kariu et al., 2006; Doolan et al., 2003.

claim: CelTOS functions to breach plasma membranes from the cytoplasmic face to enable the exit of parasites from invaded host and vector cells during traversal.
source: The results of our study indicate that CelTOS functions to breach plasma membranes from the cytoplasmic face to enable the exit of parasites from invaded host and vector cells during traversal.
evidence: Inferred from all functional and mechanistic data presented.

claim: Motility alone is not sufficient for parasite exit.
source: This study challenges the paradigm that motility alone is sufficient for parasite exit, as it is now clear that active membrane disruption by CelTOS is necessary for parasite release.
evidence: Inferred from the essential role of CelTOS in membrane disruption for traversal.

claim: Active membrane disruption by CelTOS is necessary for parasite release.
source: This study challenges the paradigm that motility alone is sufficient for parasite exit, as it is now clear that active membrane disruption by CelTOS is necessary for parasite release.
evidence: Inferred from the essential role of CelTOS and its membrane disruption activity.

claim: CelTOS-dependent pore formation leading to inner-leaflet membrane disruption is a new active molecular process during traversal.
source: This work identifies CelTOS-dependent pore formation leading to inner-leaflet membrane disruption as a new active molecular process during traversal
evidence: Inferred from the discovery of CelTOS pore formation mechanism.

claim: CelTOS defines a new class of membrane disruption proteins.
source: While CelTOS resembles viral membrane fusion proteins and a bacterial pore-forming toxin, our findings define a new class of membrane disruption proteins.
evidence: Inferred from unique structural features and mechanism compared to known membrane disruption proteins.

claim: CelTOS has a distinct structural architecture with two subdomains that independently resemble membrane binding and/or disrupting proteins.
source: CelTOS has a distinct structural architecture with two subdomains that independently resemble membrane binding and/or disrupting proteins and could simultaneously act during disruption (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: CelTOS employs a unique lipid specificity for phosphatidic acid to achieve nearly universal inner leaflet cellular activity.
source: Further, CelTOS employs a unique lipid specificity for phosphatidic acid to achieve nearly universal inner leaflet cellular activity.
evidence: Inferred from PA binding specificity and its presence in inner leaflets of diverse cells.

claim: Primary sequence similarity searches did not identify membrane disruption proteins as relatives of CelTOS.
source: This new class is also supported by the fact that primary sequence similarity searches did not identify membrane disruption proteins as relatives of CelTOS.
evidence: Stated as a result of sequence analysis.

claim: Two N-terminal helices of one CelTOS monomer pack against the C-terminal helices of a second monomer to form the dimer.
source: Two N-terminal helices (α-helices 1 and 2) of one monomer pack against the C-terminal helices (α-helices 3 and 4) of a second monomer to form the dimer.
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data.
